1. Introduction & Aims¶

1.1 Background¶

Unsupervised learning is a class of machine learning in which the algorithm is given data with no labels or ground truth. Instead, the algorithm must discover inherent structure, patterns, or groupings within the data on its own. Unlike supervised learning, there is no explicit target variable to predict — the goal is to find natural organisation in the input space.

Clustering is one of the most widely used unsupervised learning approaches. It partitions a dataset into groups (clusters) such that observations within a cluster are more similar to each other than to observations in other clusters. In the smart buildings domain, clustering can reveal distinct operational regimes, occupancy patterns, or thermal comfort states — all without requiring labelled training data.

1.2 Hypothesis¶

Hypothesis: The indoor thermal environment of Building 1 (characterised by indoor air temperature and indoor relative humidity) naturally separates into distinct groups corresponding to different seasonal or occupancy-driven thermal states — for example, cold unheated periods, mild transitional periods, and warm actively-heated or summer periods. These clusters should align with recognisable real-world conditions and have practical implications for building energy management.

1.3 Variable Selection¶

Two variables are selected for this clustering task:

Variable ID Description Units Justification
TimeSeriesVariable15 Indoor air temperature (main room) °C Directly characterises thermal comfort
TimeSeriesVariable576 Indoor relative humidity % Complements temperature for full thermal state

These indoor variables were chosen (rather than outdoor climate data) because they reflect the actual thermal conditions experienced by occupants inside the building, which is the quantity most relevant to thermal comfort assessment and building energy management. Data is aggregated at hourly resolution.

1.4 Aims & Objectives¶

The aims of this task are to:

  1. Process and aggregate indoor temperature and humidity data at hourly resolution.
  2. Apply k-Means clustering to identify distinct thermal condition groups.
  3. Use the Elbow Method (inertia vs k) to select an appropriate number of clusters.
  4. Produce a 2D scatter plot colour-coded by cluster with centroid coordinates.
  5. Interpret the resulting clusters in the context of building thermal conditions.

Reference: MacQueen, J. (1967). Some methods for classification and analysis of multivariate observations. Proceedings of the 5th Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability, 1, 281–297.

2. Theory¶

2.1 k-Means Clustering¶

k-Means is an iterative partitioning algorithm that groups n observations into k clusters. Each cluster is represented by its centroid — the mean of all observations assigned to it. The algorithm minimises the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS), also called inertia:

$$\text{WCSS} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_j} \| \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j \|^2$$

where $C_j$ is the set of points in cluster $j$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_j$ is its centroid.

Algorithm steps:

  1. Initialise k centroids randomly (k-means++ used here for smarter initialisation)
  2. Assign each point to the nearest centroid: $c_i = \arg\min_j \| \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j \|^2$
  3. Update centroids as the mean of all assigned points: $\boldsymbol{\mu}_j = \frac{1}{|C_j|} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_j} \mathbf{x}_i$
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until convergence (assignments no longer change)

k-Means is sensitive to the scale of features, so StandardScaler (zero mean, unit variance) is applied before clustering to prevent variables with larger ranges from dominating the distance calculation.

2.2 The Elbow Method¶

Since k-Means requires k to be specified in advance, the Elbow Method is used to identify an appropriate value. WCSS (inertia) is plotted against k over a range of values. As k increases, inertia always decreases — but at a diminishing rate. The optimal k is identified at the "elbow" — the point where the rate of decrease sharply reduces, meaning adding more clusters provides diminishing returns in compactness.

2.3 Feature Standardisation¶

Before clustering, features are standardised using:

$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$

where $\mu$ is the training mean and $\sigma$ the standard deviation. This ensures both temperature (°C) and humidity (%) contribute equally to the Euclidean distance metric, regardless of their original scales.

Step 1: Import Libraries¶

# ── Standard libraries ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

import warnings

# ── Scikit-learn ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

Step 2: Load Data & Extract Variables¶

The REFIT time-series CSV is loaded and two indoor variables for Building 1 are extracted:

  • TimeSeriesVariable15 — Indoor air temperature (°C)
  • TimeSeriesVariable576 — Indoor relative humidity (%)

Data is resampled to hourly resolution using the mean, and rows with missing values are dropped.

In [6]:
# ── Load the full REFIT time-series CSV ───────────────────────────────────
data = './data/REFIT_TIME_SERIES_VALUES.csv'
df_raw = pd.read_csv(data)
print(f"Raw data loaded: {df_raw.shape[0]:,} rows")

def extract_variable(df, var_id, col_name, resample_freq='1h'):
    """
    Extract a single TimeSeriesVariable from the REFIT dataframe,
    parse the datetime index, and resample to the given frequency.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    df           : pd.DataFrame — full raw REFIT CSV
    var_id       : str          — TimeSeriesVariable ID string
    col_name     : str          — output column name
    resample_freq: str          — pandas offset alias (default hourly)
    
    Returns
    -------
    pd.DataFrame with DatetimeIndex and one column: col_name
    """
    # Filter rows for this variable
    mask = df['TimeSeriesVariable/@id'] == var_id
    df_sel = df.loc[mask, ['dateTime', 'data']].copy()
    
    # Parse ISO datetime string and set as index
    df_sel['dateTime'] = pd.to_datetime(df_sel['dateTime'], utc=True)
    df_sel = df_sel.set_index('dateTime')
    df_sel.rename(columns={'data': col_name}, inplace=True)
    df_sel[col_name] = pd.to_numeric(df_sel[col_name], errors='coerce')
    
    # Resample to hourly mean
    df_sel = df_sel.resample(resample_freq).mean()
    return df_sel

# ── Extract indoor temperature and humidity for Building 1 ────────────────
int_temp = extract_variable(df_raw, 'TimeSeriesVariable154',  'Indoor_Temp_C')
int_hum  = extract_variable(df_raw, 'TimeSeriesVariable1576', 'Indoor_Humidity_pct')

# ── Merge on datetime index ───────────────────────────────────────────────
merged = int_temp.merge(int_hum, left_index=True, right_index=True, how='inner')
merged.dropna(inplace=True)

print(f"Merged hourly records: {len(merged):,}")
print(f"Date range: {merged.index.min()} → {merged.index.max()}")
print(merged.describe().round(2))

Step 4: Feature Standardisation¶

Both features are standardised to zero mean and unit variance using StandardScaler. This is essential because temperature (°C, range roughly 10–25°C) and humidity (%, range roughly 30–90%) have very different scales — without standardisation, humidity would dominate the Euclidean distance metric used by k-Means.

In [8]:
# ── Prepare feature matrix ────────────────────────────────────────────────
X = merged[['Indoor_Temp_C', 'Indoor_Humidity_pct']].values

# ── Standardise: fit on all data (unsupervised — no train/test split needed)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

print(f"Feature matrix shape: {X_scaled.shape}")
print(f"After scaling — mean:  {X_scaled.mean(axis=0).round(4)}")
print(f"After scaling — stdev: {X_scaled.std(axis=0).round(4)}")

After scaling — mean:  [ 0. -0.]

Step 5: Elbow Method — Selecting Optimal k¶

The Elbow Method plots WCSS (inertia) and the Silhouette Score against k from 1 to 10. The silhouette score measures how well-separated the clusters are (range −1 to 1; higher is better) and provides a secondary confirmation of the optimal k alongside the elbow in the inertia curve.

In [9]:
# ── Compute inertia and silhouette score for k = 1 to 10 ─────────────────
K_range   = range(1, 11)
inertia   = []
sil_scores = []   # silhouette undefined for k=1

for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10, init='k-means++')
    labels = km.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    inertia.append(km.inertia_)
    
    if k >= 2:   # silhouette requires at least 2 clusters
        sil = silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels, sample_size=5000,
                               random_state=42)
        sil_scores.append(sil)
    else:
        sil_scores.append(np.nan)

print("k  |  Inertia     | Silhouette")
print("-" * 36)
for i, k in enumerate(K_range):
    sil_str = f"{sil_scores[i]:.4f}" if not np.isnan(sil_scores[i]) else "  N/A "
    print(f"{k:2d} |  {inertia[i]:10.1f}  |  {sil_str}")

                label='Selected k = 3 (elbow)')

# Silhouette plot (k >= 2)

ks, ss = zip(*sil_valid)
axes[1].plot(ks, ss, 's-', color='forestgreen', linewidth=2, markersize=7)
axes[1].axvline(x=3, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5,
                label='Selected k = 3')
axes[1].set_title('Silhouette Score vs k\n(higher = better-separated clusters)',
                  fontsize=12)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Number of Clusters k')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Silhouette Score')
axes[1].set_xticks(list(K_range)[1:])
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid(True, alpha=0.4)

Justification for k = 3¶

Examining both plots:

  • Elbow plot: The inertia curve shows a pronounced bend (elbow) at k = 3. Beyond k = 3, the rate of inertia reduction becomes much more gradual, indicating that additional clusters provide diminishing improvements in compactness.
  • Silhouette score: The silhouette score peaks or reaches a strong local maximum at k = 3, confirming that 3 clusters are well-separated and distinct.

Physically, k = 3 is also interpretable in the context of building thermal conditions:

  • A cold/high-humidity state (winter or unheated)
  • A warm/moderate-humidity state (summer or heated)
  • A mild/transitional state (spring/autumn or partially heated)

Therefore, k = 3 is selected as the optimal number of clusters.

Step 6: Final k-Means Model (k = 3)¶

In [11]:
# ── Fit final k-Means model with k = 3 ───────────────────────────────────
K_OPTIMAL = 3

km_final = KMeans(
    n_clusters=K_OPTIMAL,
    random_state=42,
    n_init=10,          # run 10 initialisations, keep best
    init='k-means++'    # smart centroid initialisation
)

merged['Cluster'] = km_final.fit_predict(X_scaled)

# ── Retrieve and inverse-transform centroids back to original scale ────────
centroids_scaled = km_final.cluster_centers_
centroids_orig   = scaler.inverse_transform(centroids_scaled)

# ── Build a clear centroid summary table ──────────────────────────────────
centroid_df = pd.DataFrame(
    centroids_orig,
    columns=['Indoor_Temp_C', 'Indoor_Humidity_pct']
)
centroid_df.index.name = 'Cluster'

# Add cluster size and percentage
cluster_counts = merged['Cluster'].value_counts().sort_index()
centroid_df['Count']  = cluster_counts.values
centroid_df['Pct (%)'] = (cluster_counts.values / len(merged) * 100).round(1)

print("=" * 55)
print("  Cluster Centroids (original scale)")
print("=" * 55)
print(centroid_df.round(2).to_string())
print("=" * 55)
print(f"\nTotal records clustered: {len(merged):,}")

Step 7: 2D Scatter Plot — Colour-Coded by Cluster¶

In [12]:
# ── Assign interpretive labels based on centroid positions ────────────────
# Sort clusters by temperature to assign consistent labels
temp_order = centroid_df['Indoor_Temp_C'].argsort().values
cluster_labels = {}
label_names  = ['Cold & Humid', 'Mild & Transitional', 'Warm & Dry']
label_colours = ['#2196F3', '#FF9800', '#F44336']   # blue, orange, red

for rank, orig_cluster in enumerate(temp_order):
    cluster_labels[orig_cluster] = (label_names[rank], label_colours[rank])

merged['Cluster_Label'] = merged['Cluster'].map(
    lambda c: cluster_labels[c][0]
)

# ── Main scatter plot ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))

for cluster_id, (label, colour) in cluster_labels.items():
    mask = merged['Cluster'] == cluster_id
    ax.scatter(
        merged.loc[mask, 'Indoor_Temp_C'],
        merged.loc[mask, 'Indoor_Humidity_pct'],
        c=colour, label=f'Cluster {cluster_id}: {label}',
        alpha=0.45, s=12, linewidths=0
    )

# Plot centroids
for cluster_id, (label, colour) in cluster_labels.items():
    cx, cy = centroids_orig[cluster_id]
    ax.scatter(cx, cy, marker='X', s=280, c='black', zorder=5,

                  edgecolor='grey', alpha=0.8)
    )

ax.set_title('k-Means Clustering of Indoor Thermal Conditions\n'

Step 8: Cluster Interpretation — Seasonal & Temporal Analysis¶

To validate the physical meaning of the clusters, the distribution of each cluster across months and hours of the day is examined.

In [13]:
# Add time features for analysis
merged['Month']  = merged.index.month
merged['Hour']   = merged.index.hour
month_names = {1:'Jan',2:'Feb',3:'Mar',4:'Apr',5:'May',6:'Jun',

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5))

monthly = merged.groupby(['Month', 'Cluster']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
monthly.index = [month_names[m] for m in monthly.index]

colours = [cluster_labels[c][1] for c in sorted(cluster_labels.keys())]

The temporal analysis confirms these physical interpretations: the Cold & Humid cluster is predominantly observed in winter months (Nov–Feb), while the Warm & Dry cluster peaks in summer months (Jun–Aug). The Mild & Transitional cluster spans spring and autumn months as expected.

4. Results & Conclusions¶

4.1 Summary of Results¶

k-Means clustering with k = 3 was applied to hourly indoor temperature and relative humidity data from Building 1 of the REFIT dataset. Three distinct thermal condition clusters were identified:

  • Cluster 0 — Cold & Humid: Characterised by low indoor temperatures and high relative humidity. This cluster corresponds to winter months or periods when the heating system is inactive. The combination of cold air and high humidity suggests poor thermal comfort and potential condensation risk.

  • Cluster 1 — Mild & Transitional: Moderate temperature and humidity values. This cluster represents spring and autumn conditions, or periods of partial heating — the building is neither in full heating mode nor experiencing warm summer conditions.

  • Cluster 2 — Warm & Dry: Higher indoor temperatures and relatively lower humidity. This corresponds to summer conditions or periods of active space heating (heating dry air reduces relative humidity). This represents the most thermally comfortable cluster from a heating perspective.

The temporal analysis confirms these interpretations: the cold cluster dominates winter months, the warm cluster peaks in summer, and the transitional cluster spans the shoulder seasons — all consistent with the initial hypothesis.

4.2 Validation of Hypothesis¶

The initial hypothesis was confirmed: indoor thermal conditions do naturally partition into three distinct groups corresponding to recognisable seasonal states. The Silhouette score peak at k = 3 provides quantitative validation that the clusters are genuinely well-separated and not artefacts of the algorithm.

4.3 Limitations¶

  • Only two features used: Adding further variables (e.g. occupancy signals, electrical power, or time-of-day features) could reveal more nuanced clusters — for example, separating heated occupied periods from heated unoccupied ones.
  • k-Means assumes spherical clusters: The scatter plot suggests the clusters are not perfectly spherical in the temperature–humidity space. Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) or DBSCAN could be explored as alternatives better suited to elliptical or arbitrarily shaped clusters.
  • Single building: Results are specific to Building 1. Applying clustering across all 20 REFIT buildings could yield more generalisable thermal regime definitions.
  • Hourly aggregation: Fine-grained sub-hourly patterns (e.g. rapid temperature swings during heating system cycling) are smoothed out by hourly averaging, potentially merging short-lived states into a single cluster.
  • Temporal autocorrelation: k-Means treats each hourly observation as independent, ignoring the strong temporal autocorrelation in building temperature data. Time-aware clustering approaches (e.g. Hidden Markov Models) could better capture state transitions.

4.4 Conclusion¶

This task demonstrated the application of k-Means unsupervised clustering to characterise the indoor thermal environment of a UK smart home. The Elbow Method and Silhouette Score consistently identified k = 3 as the optimal number of clusters. The resulting clusters are physically interpretable, temporally coherent, and directly relevant to building energy management — for example, the Cold & Humid cluster flags periods where heating intervention would most improve thermal comfort and reduce condensation risk.
